questionText: For a given traffic stream, the speed-density relationship is given as: $v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)$ where $v$ is the mean speed (in km/h) and $k$ is the density (in veh/km).Considering $v_o = 45$ km/h and $k_j = 200$ veh/km, the maximum flow (in veh/h) for the given stream is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
explanationHtml:
Given speed-density model: v=voln⁡(kjk)v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)v=vo​ln(kkj​​)

where vo=45v_o = 45vo​=45 km/h, kj=200k_j = 200kj​=200 veh/km

Step 1 - Flow = speed x density:
q=v⋅k=voln⁡(kjk)⋅kq = v \cdot k = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) \cdot kq=v⋅k=vo​ln(kkj​​)⋅k

Step 2 - Maximize flow dqdk=0\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0dkdq​=0:
dqdk=vo[ln⁡(kjk)+k⋅(−1k)]=vo[ln⁡(kjk)−1]=0\dfrac{dq}{dk} = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) + k \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)\right] = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) - 1\right] = 0dkdq​=vo​[ln(kkj​​)+k⋅(−k1​)]=vo​[ln(kkj​​)−1]=0
ln⁡(kjk)=1⇒kjk=e⇒k∗=kje=200e=2002.718=73.57\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{k_j}{k} = e \Rightarrow k^* = \dfrac{k_j}{e} = \dfrac{200}{e} = \dfrac{200}{2.718} = 73.57ln(kkj​​)=1⇒kkj​​=e⇒k∗=ekj​​=e200​=2.718200​=73.57 veh/km

Step 3 - Speed at maximum flow:
v∗=voln⁡(kjk∗)=45×ln⁡(e)=45×1=45v^* = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k^*}\right) = 45 \times \ln(e) = 45 \times 1 = 45v∗=vo​ln(k∗kj​​)=45×ln(e)=45×1=45 km/h

Step 4 - Maximum flow:
qmax=v∗×k∗=45×73.57=3311 veh/hq_{max} = v^* \times k^* = 45 \times 73.57 = \mathbf{3311 \text{ veh/h}}qmax​=v∗×k∗=45×73.57=3311 veh/h
explanationText: Given speed-density model: $v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)$ where $v_o = 45$ km/h, $k_j = 200$ veh/kmStep 1 - Flow = speed x density: $q = v \cdot k = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) \cdot k$ Step 2 - Maximize flow $\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0$ : $\dfrac{dq}{dk} = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) + k \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)\right] = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) - 1\right] = 0$ $\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{k_j}{k} = e \Rightarrow k^* = \dfrac{k_j}{e} = \dfrac{200}{e} = \dfrac{200}{2.718} = 73.57$ veh/kmStep 3 - Speed at maximum flow: $v^* = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k^*}\right) = 45 \times \ln(e) = 45 \times 1 = 45$ km/hStep 4 - Maximum flow: $q_{max} = v^* \times k^* = 45 \times 73.57 = \mathbf{3311 \text{ veh/h}}$

questionMarkup: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the type of stresses to be considered for the design of rigid pavements?
questionText: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the type of stresses to be considered for the design of rigid pavements?

options.html: Warping stress due to temperature differential between top and bottom of the pavement slab as a result of daily variation in temperature
options.text: Warping stress due to temperature differential between top and bottom of the pavement slab as a result of daily variation in temperature

options.html: Frictional stress due to overall increase or decrease in temperature of the pavement slab as a result of seasonal variation in temperature
options.text: Frictional stress due to overall increase or decrease in temperature of the pavement slab as a result of seasonal variation in temperature

options.html: Critical stress obtained as the maximum of the wheel load stress, the warping stress, and the frictional stress
options.text: Critical stress obtained as the maximum of the wheel load stress, the warping stress, and the frictional stress

options.html: Critical stress obtained as the sum of wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner of the pavement slab
options.text: Critical stress obtained as the sum of wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner of the pavement slab

explanationHtml:
Option A:
Warping stresses develop in a rigid pavement due to the temperature difference between the top and bottom surfaces of the slab during a day.
The temperature gradient causes the slab to curl upward or downward, producing warping stresses.

Therefore,Option A is TRUE \boxed{\text{Option A is TRUE}} Option A is TRUE​
Option B:
Seasonal changes in temperature cause the entire slab to expand or contract. Since the slab movement is restrained by subgrade friction, frictional stresses are developed.

Therefore,Option B is TRUE \boxed{\text{Option B is TRUE}} Option B is TRUE​
Option C:

In rigid pavement design, the critical tensile stress is not obtained by taking the maximum of wheel load stress, warping stress, and frictional stress individually.
The design stress is generally obtained by combining the wheel load stress and temperature-related stresses at the critical location.
Hence, taking only the maximum of the individual stresses is incorrect.

Therefore,Option C is FALSE \boxed{\text{Option C is FALSE}} Option C is FALSE​
Option D:

Wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner do not occur simultaneously at the same location.
The critical condition is obtained by considering the most critical loading position, not by summing all three stresses.

Therefore,Option D is FALSE \boxed{\text{Option D is FALSE}} Option D is FALSE​
explanationText: Option A:Warping stresses develop in a rigid pavement due to the temperature difference between the top and bottom surfaces of the slab during a day.The temperature gradient causes the slab to curl upward or downward, producing warping stresses.Therefore, $\boxed{\text{Option A is TRUE}}$ Option B:Seasonal changes in temperature cause the entire slab to expand or contract. Since the slab movement is restrained by subgrade friction, frictional stresses are developed.Therefore, $\boxed{\text{Option B is TRUE}}$ Option C:In rigid pavement design, the critical tensile stress is not obtained by taking the maximum of wheel load stress, warping stress, and frictional stress individually.The design stress is generally obtained by combining the wheel load stress and temperature-related stresses at the critical location.Hence, taking only the maximum of the individual stresses is incorrect.Therefore, $\boxed{\text{Option C is FALSE}}$ Option D:Wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner do not occur simultaneously at the same location.The critical condition is obtained by considering the most critical loading position, not by summing all three stresses.Therefore, $\boxed{\text{Option D is FALSE}}$

Statement-2: Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC) in rigid pavements is caused due to repeated cycles of axle loads and negative temperature differential.

The CORRECT option is:
questionText: Consider the following statements with respect to rigid pavements:Statement-1: Bottom-up cracking (BUC) in rigid pavements is caused at the edge of the slab due to combined effect of single or tandem rear axle load and positive temperature differential.Statement-2: Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC) in rigid pavements is caused due to repeated cycles of axle loads and negative temperature differential.The CORRECT option is:

options.html: Statement-1 is TRUE but Statement-2 is FALSE.
options.text: Statement-1 is TRUE but Statement-2 is FALSE.

options.html: Statement-1 is FALSE but Statement-2 is TRUE.
options.text: Statement-1 is FALSE but Statement-2 is TRUE.

explanationHtml:
Statement 1 - Bottom-up cracking (BUC):
BUC initiates at the bottom of the slab where tensile stresses are maximum. It is caused by:
Heavy axle loads (single or tandem rear axle) causing bending stress - maximum tension at bottom
Positive temperature differential (top > bottom) causes the slab to curl upward at edges/corners, making the slab unsupported at edges - this increases bottom tensile stress
Statement 1 is TRUE.

Statement 2 - Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC):
TDC initiates at the top surface of the slab and propagates downward. It is caused by:
Repeated cycles of axle loads on the slab surface
Negative temperature differential (bottom > top) causes slab to curl downward at edges - top surface is in tension, initiating top-down cracks
Statement 2 is TRUE.

Therefore, Both statements are TRUE.
explanationText: Statement 1 - Bottom-up cracking (BUC):BUC initiates at the bottom of the slab where tensile stresses are maximum. It is caused by: Heavy axle loads (single or tandem rear axle) causing bending stress - maximum tension at bottom Positive temperature differential (top > bottom) causes the slab to curl upward at edges/corners, making the slab unsupported at edges - this increases bottom tensile stress Statement 1 is TRUE.Statement 2 - Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC):TDC initiates at the top surface of the slab and propagates downward. It is caused by: Repeated cycles of axle loads on the slab surface Negative temperature differential (bottom > top) causes slab to curl downward at edges - top surface is in tension, initiating top-down cracks Statement 2 is TRUE.Therefore, Both statements are TRUE.

questionText: A downgrade of 1 in 100 meets an upgrade of 1 in 125 on a road. If the rate of change of grade is 0.10% per 30 m, the length (in m) of the vertical curve between the two grades is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
explanationHtml:
Given:
Downgrade: −1/100=−1%-1/100 = -1\%−1/100=−1%
Upgrade: +1/125=+0.8%+1/125 = +0.8\%+1/125=+0.8%
Rate of change of grade: r=0.10%r = 0.10\%r=0.10% per 30 m

Step 1 - Total change in grade (algebraic difference):
From −1%-1\%−1% to +0.8%+0.8\%+0.8%:
N=g2−g1=+0.8−(−1.0)=1.8%N = g_2 - g_1 = +0.8 - (-1.0) = 1.8\%N=g2​−g1​=+0.8−(−1.0)=1.8%

Step 2 - Length of vertical curve:
L=Nr×30=1.80.10×30=18×30=540 mL = \dfrac{N}{r} \times 30 = \dfrac{1.8}{0.10} \times 30 = 18 \times 30 = \mathbf{540 \text{ m}}L=rN​×30=0.101.8​×30=18×30=540 m
explanationText: Given:Downgrade: $-1/100 = -1\%$ Upgrade: $+1/125 = +0.8\%$ Rate of change of grade: $r = 0.10\%$ per 30 mStep 1 - Total change in grade (algebraic difference):From $-1\%$ to $+0.8\%$ : $N = g_2 - g_1 = +0.8 - (-1.0) = 1.8\%$ Step 2 - Length of vertical curve: $L = \dfrac{N}{r} \times 30 = \dfrac{1.8}{0.10} \times 30 = 18 \times 30 = \mathbf{540 \text{ m}}$

Traffic is moving on a 6-lane dual carriageway road. Traffic volume per direction during peak hour (08:00 am to 09:00 am) is 6000 veh/h. It is assumed that the traffic is distributed uniformly across the lanes in each direction. Just at 08:00 am, a truck goes out of order on the middle lane of one side, thus disrupting the traffic on that lane in one direction. The lane capacity under normal conditions is 2000 veh/h/ln and under queue formation it is 1600 veh/h/ln. The traffic resumes at 08:30 am on removing the truck from the middle lane. Hourly traffic volume after 09:00 am reduces to 5000 veh/h/dir.

The number of  vehicles in the queue at 10:00 am is ______ (in integer).
questionText: Traffic is moving on a 6-lane dual carriageway road. Traffic volume per direction during peak hour (08:00 am to 09:00 am) is 6000 veh/h. It is assumed that the traffic is distributed uniformly across the lanes in each direction. Just at 08:00 am, a truck goes out of order on the middle lane of one side, thus disrupting the traffic on that lane in one direction. The lane capacity under normal conditions is 2000 veh/h/ln and under queue formation it is 1600 veh/h/ln. The traffic resumes at 08:30 am on removing the truck from the middle lane. Hourly traffic volume after 09:00 am reduces to 5000 veh/h/dir. The number of vehicles in the queue at 10:00 am is ______ (in integer).
explanationHtml:
Phase 1: 08:00 am to 08:30 am (Incident Period)

Arrival rate:λ1=6000 veh/h \lambda_1=6000\ \text{veh/h} λ1​=6000 veh/h
Number of open lanes:3−1=2 lanes 3-1=2\ \text{lanes} 3−1=2 lanes
Capacity under queue conditions:C1=2×1600=3200 veh/h C_1=2\times1600=3200\ \text{veh/h} C1​=2×1600=3200 veh/h
Queue accumulation rate:λ1−C1=6000−3200=2800 veh/h \lambda_1-C_1 = 6000-3200 = 2800\ \text{veh/h} λ1​−C1​=6000−3200=2800 veh/h
Queue at 08:30 am:=2800×0.5=1400 vehicles = 2800\times0.5 = 1400\ \text{vehicles} =2800×0.5=1400 vehicles

Phase 2: 08:30 am to 09:00 am (Post-Incident Peak Hour)

Arrival rate:λ1=6000 veh/h \lambda_1=6000\ \text{veh/h} λ1​=6000 veh/h
All three lanes are reopened.

Since a queue already exists, the lanes discharge at queue capacity:
C2=3×1600=4800 veh/h C_2 = 3\times1600 = 4800\ \text{veh/h} C2​=3×1600=4800 veh/h

Queue accumulation rate:

questionMarkup: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE in the context of the geometric design of highways?
questionText: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE in the context of the geometric design of highways?

options.html:
The coefficient of friction used for the design of horizontal curves is lower than the
coefficient of friction used in the computation of the sight distances.
options.text: The coefficient of friction used for the design of horizontal curves is lower than the coefficient of friction used in the computation of the sight distances.

options.html:
Centrifugal force at horizontal curve is counteracted by raising the middle of the
pavement with respect to the edges.
options.text: Centrifugal force at horizontal curve is counteracted by raising the middle of the pavement with respect to the edges.

options.html: Grade compensation is achieved by increasing the gradient of the horizontal curve.
options.text: Grade compensation is achieved by increasing the gradient of the horizontal curve.

options.html:
Under identical conditions, the design length of the summit curve of a road having
unidirectional flow will be greater than that of the same road having bidirectional
flow.
options.text: Under identical conditions, the design length of the summit curve of a road having unidirectional flow will be greater than that of the same road having bidirectional flow.

explanationHtml:
(A) TRUE: Coefficient of friction for horizontal curve design (f = 0.10-0.15) is indeed lower than that used for sight distance/braking (f = 0.35-0.40). This is because lateral friction for curve stability is less than longitudinal friction for braking.

(B) FALSE: Centrifugal force is counteracted by raising the outer edge of the pavement (superelevation/cant), not the middle.

(C) FALSE: Grade compensation means reducing (not increasing) the gradient on horizontal curves to compensate for the extra resistance due to curvature.

(D) FALSE: For unidirectional flow, the stopping sight distance (SSD) is used, which is shorter than the overtaking sight distance (OSD) used for bidirectional flow. Summit curve length ∝\propto∝ SSD² or OSD². Since OSD > SSD, bidirectional needs longer curve. So unidirectional summit curve is shorter, not longer.
explanationText: (A) TRUE: Coefficient of friction for horizontal curve design (f = 0.10-0.15) is indeed lower than that used for sight distance/braking (f = 0.35-0.40). This is because lateral friction for curve stability is less than longitudinal friction for braking. (B) FALSE: Centrifugal force is counteracted by raising the outer edge of the pavement (superelevation/cant), not the middle. (C) FALSE: Grade compensation means reducing (not increasing) the gradient on horizontal curves to compensate for the extra resistance due to curvature. (D) FALSE: For unidirectional flow, the stopping sight distance (SSD) is used, which is shorter than the overtaking sight distance (OSD) used for bidirectional flow. Summit curve length $\propto$ SSD² or OSD². Since OSD > SSD, bidirectional needs longer curve. So unidirectional summit curve is shorter, not longer.

questionText: A road is divided into four sections having varying widths as shown in the figure. Section-2 (S2) represents a capacity constrained condition with respect to the traffic flow passing through Section-1 (S1). Section-3 (S3) and Section-4 (S4) do not face any such capacity constraint with respect to the flow. A flow-density relationship for unconstrained and constrained flow conditions is shown in the figure.If Section-1 observes density $D_2$ , the option representing the correct state of density in Sections 2, 3 and 4 is:
explanationHtml:
Analysis using flow-density diagram:

S1 has density D2 → \rightarrow → operating on the unconstrained (free flow) curve at point 2.

S2 is capacity-constrained (bottleneck). Flow entering S2 equals flow at S1. Since S2 is constrained, it operates on the constrained flow curve at the same flow level → \rightarrow → this corresponds to density D4 (high density, congested).

S3 is downstream of bottleneck, unconstrained. Flow rate drops to capacity of S2 → \rightarrow → S3 operates on unconstrained curve at that lower flow → \rightarrow → density D3.

S4 is further downstream, unconstrained, same flow as S3 → \rightarrow → density D2 (same as S1, back to free flow).

Therefore, S2 → \rightarrow → D4 ; S3 → \rightarrow → D3 ; S4 → \rightarrow → D2

questionText: The travel times of three vehicles on a 2 km stretch of road are 4, 5, and 8 minutes. Assuming the speed of each vehicle to be constant in this stretch, the Space Mean Speed (in km/h) of the vehicles is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Space Mean Speed (SMS) is the harmonic mean of individual speeds.

Given: Distance = 2 km, Travel times = 4, 5, 8 minutes

Step 1 - Individual speeds:
v1=2 km4/60 h=30 km/hv_1 = \dfrac{2 \text{ km}}{4/60 \text{ h}} = 30 \text{ km/h}v1​=4/60 h2 km​=30 km/h
v2=25/60=24 km/hv_2 = \dfrac{2}{5/60} = 24 \text{ km/h}v2​=5/602​=24 km/h
v3=28/60=15 km/hv_3 = \dfrac{2}{8/60} = 15 \text{ km/h}v3​=8/602​=15 km/h

Step 2 - Space Mean Speed (harmonic mean):
SMS=n∑1vi=3130+124+115SMS = \dfrac{n}{\sum \dfrac{1}{v_i}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{15}}SMS=∑vi​1​n​=301​+241​+151​3​

=34120+5120+8120=317120=3×12017=36017=21.18 km/h= \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{4}{120} + \dfrac{5}{120} + \dfrac{8}{120}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{17}{120}} = \dfrac{3 \times 120}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} = \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}=1204​+1205​+1208​3​=12017​3​=173×120​=17360​=21.18 km/h

Alternatively: SMS=Total distanceAverage travel time=2(4+5+8)/(3×60)=2×3×6017=36017≈21.18 km/hSMS = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Average travel time}} = \dfrac{2}{(4+5+8)/(3 \times 60)} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 \times 60}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} \approx \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}SMS=Average travel timeTotal distance​=(4+5+8)/(3×60)2​=172×3×60​=17360​≈21.18 km/h
explanationText: Space Mean Speed (SMS) is the harmonic mean of individual speeds.Given: Distance = 2 km, Travel times = 4, 5, 8 minutesStep 1 - Individual speeds: $v_1 = \dfrac{2 \text{ km}}{4/60 \text{ h}} = 30 \text{ km/h}$ $v_2 = \dfrac{2}{5/60} = 24 \text{ km/h}$ $v_3 = \dfrac{2}{8/60} = 15 \text{ km/h}$ Step 2 - Space Mean Speed (harmonic mean): $SMS = \dfrac{n}{\sum \dfrac{1}{v_i}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{15}}$ $= \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{4}{120} + \dfrac{5}{120} + \dfrac{8}{120}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{17}{120}} = \dfrac{3 \times 120}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} = \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}$ Alternatively: $SMS = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Average travel time}} = \dfrac{2}{(4+5+8)/(3 \times 60)} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 \times 60}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} \approx \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}$

questionText: Cant $C$ on a Broad Gauge railway track is calculated for an equilibrium speed $V$ (in km/h), dynamic gauge $G$ (in mm) and radius of curve $R$ (in m) using formula/formulae:

options.html: C=GV2127RC = \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}C=127RGV2​
C=13.76 V2RC = \dfrac{13.76\, V^2}{R}C=R13.76V2​
C=13.20 V2RC = \dfrac{13.20\, V^2}{R}C=R13.20V2​
C=8.33 V2RC = \dfrac{8.33\, V^2}{R}C=R8.33V2​

explanationHtml:
Derivation of Cant formula:

For a vehicle travelling at speed VVV km/h on a curve of radius RRR metres:

Centrifugal acceleration =V2R= \dfrac{V^2}{R}=RV2​ (in appropriate units)

For equilibrium, the cant (superelevation) CCC is: GV2gR \dfrac{GV^2}{gR}gRGV2​

Converting V from km/h to m/s: Vm/s=Vkm/h3.6V_{m/s} = \dfrac{V_{km/h}}{3.6}Vm/s​=3.6Vkm/h​​

C=G⋅(V3.6)29.81⋅R=GV29.81×12.96×R=GV2127.1R≈GV2127RC = \dfrac{G \cdot \left(\dfrac{V}{3.6}\right)^2}{9.81 \cdot R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{9.81 \times 12.96 \times R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{127.1 R} \approx \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}C=9.81⋅RG⋅(3.6V​)2​=9.81×12.96×RGV2​=127.1RGV2​≈127RGV2​

where G = dynamic gauge in mm, V in km/h, R in m.

This is the standard Indian Railways formula for cant on Broad Gauge.
explanationText: Derivation of Cant formula:For a vehicle travelling at speed $V$ km/h on a curve of radius $R$ metres:Centrifugal acceleration $= \dfrac{V^2}{R}$ (in appropriate units)For equilibrium, the cant (superelevation) $C$ is: $\dfrac{GV^2}{gR}$ Converting V from km/h to m/s: $V_{m/s} = \dfrac{V_{km/h}}{3.6}$ $C = \dfrac{G \cdot \left(\dfrac{V}{3.6}\right)^2}{9.81 \cdot R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{9.81 \times 12.96 \times R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{127.1 R} \approx \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}$ where G = dynamic gauge in mm, V in km/h, R in m.This is the standard Indian Railways formula for cant on Broad Gauge.

Standard ICAO corrections to basic runway length:

The Back Bearing of line ABABAB, and

FB of AB=60∘ \text{FB of } AB = 60^\circ FB of AB=60∘
BB of AB=60∘+180∘=240∘ \text{BB of } AB = 60^\circ + 180^\circ = 240^\circ BB of AB=60∘+180∘=240∘

Step 2: Given Fore Bearing of BC
FB of BC=122∘ \text{FB of } BC = 122^\circ FB of BC=122∘

questionText: On a two-lane highway, a horizontal curve of radius $300\ \text{m}$ is provided. The design speed is $80\ \text{km/h}$ . explanationHtml:
As per IRC, extra widening on a horizontal curve is given by the formula:
We=Wm+WphW_e = W_m + W_{ph}We​=Wm​+Wph​
Where:
Wm=mechanical widening=nl22RW_m = \text{mechanical widening} = \frac{n l^2}{2R}Wm​=mechanical widening=2Rnl2​
Wph=psychological widening=v9.5RW_{ph} = \text{psychological widening} = \frac{v}{9.5 \sqrt{R}}Wph​=psychological widening=9.5R​v​

Given:
n=2, l=7 m, R=300 m, v=80 km/hn = 2,\ l = 7\ \text{m},\ R = 300\ \text{m},\ v = 80\ \text{km/h}n=2, l=7 m, R=300 m, v=80 km/h

Step 1: Mechanical Widening
Wm=2×722×300=98600=0.1633 mW_m = \frac{2 \times 7^2}{2 \times 300} = \frac{98}{600} = 0.1633\ \text{m}Wm​=2×3002×72​=60098​=0.1633 m

Step 2: Psychological Widening
R=300≈17.32\sqrt{R} = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.32R​=300​≈17.32
Wph=809.5×17.32=80164.54≈0.4863 mW_{ph} = \frac{80}{9.5 \times 17.32} = \frac{80}{164.54} \approx 0.4863\ \text{m}Wph​=9.5×17.3280​=164.5480​≈0.4863 m

Step 3: Total Extra Widening
We=0.1633+0.4863=0.65 mW_e = 0.1633 + 0.4863 = \boxed{0.65\ \text{m}}We​=0.1633+0.4863=0.65 m​
explanationText: As per IRC, extra widening on a horizontal curve is given by the formula: $W_e = W_m + W_{ph}$ Where: $W_m = \text{mechanical widening} = \frac{n l^2}{2R}$ $W_{ph} = \text{psychological widening} = \frac{v}{9.5 \sqrt{R}}$ Given: $n = 2,\ l = 7\ \text{m},\ R = 300\ \text{m},\ v = 80\ \text{km/h}$ Step 1: Mechanical Widening $W_m = \frac{2 \times 7^2}{2 \times 300} = \frac{98}{600} = 0.1633\ \text{m}$ Step 2: Psychological Widening $\sqrt{R} = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.32$ $W_{ph} = \frac{80}{9.5 \times 17.32} = \frac{80}{164.54} \approx 0.4863\ \text{m}$ Step 3: Total Extra Widening $W_e = 0.1633 + 0.4863 = \boxed{0.65\ \text{m}}$

explanationHtml:

v=Vf(1−kkj)=100(1−2000/v160) v = V_f \left(1 - \frac{k}{k_j}\right) = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000/v}{160}\right) v=Vf​(1−kj​k​)=100(1−1602000/v​)

Solving this quadratic:
v=100±1002−4⋅1⋅125002=100±10000−500002=100±−400002 v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 12500}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 50000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{-40000}}{2} v=2100±1002−4⋅1⋅12500​​=2100±10000−50000​​=2100±−40000​​

Correct equation:
Go back to:
v=100(1−2000160v) v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v} \right) v=100(1−160v2000​)

So:

5000≈70.71 \sqrt{5000} \approx 70.71 5000​≈70.71

explanationText: Given: Free flow speed $V_f = 100 \text{ km/h}$ Capacity $Q_{\text{max}} = 4000 \text{ veh/h}$ Flow $Q = 2000 \text{ veh/h}$ In a linear speed-density relationship: $Q = k \cdot v$ Where: $k$ is the density $v$ is the speedMaximum flow (capacity) occurs at: $k = k_j / 2 \quad \text{and} \quad v = V_f / 2$ So at capacity: $Q_{\text{max}} = (k_j/2)(V_f/2) = \frac{k_j V_f}{4}$ Solving for $k_j$ : $k_j = \frac{4 Q_{\text{max}}}{V_f} = \frac{4 \cdot 4000}{100} = 160 \text{ veh/km}$ Now for given flow $Q = 2000$ : Let $v$ be the possible speed: $Q = k \cdot v \Rightarrow 2000 = k \cdot v \Rightarrow k = \frac{2000}{v}$ From linear speed-density relation: $v = V_f \left(1 - \frac{k}{k_j}\right) = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000/v}{160}\right)$ $v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v}\right)$ Multiply both sides by $160v$ : $160v^2 = 16000v - 2000000$ $v^2 - 100v + 12500 = 0$ Solving this quadratic: $v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 12500}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 50000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{-40000}}{2}$ Oops! That's an error! Let's fix it: Correct equation: Go back to: $v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v} \right)$ $v = 100 - \frac{200000}{160v}$ Multiply both sides by $v$ : $v^2 = 100v - \frac{200000}{160} = 100v - 1250$ So: $v^2 - 100v + 1250 = 0$ Now solving: $v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 1250}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 5000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{5000}}{2}$ $\sqrt{5000} \approx 70.71$ $v = \frac{100 \pm 70.71}{2}$ $v_1 = \frac{100 + 70.71}{2} = 85.36 \text{ km/h}$ $v_2 = \frac{100 - 70.71}{2} = 14.64 \text{ km/h}$ So, possible speeds are: $\boxed{85.36 \text{ km/h},\ 14.64 \text{ km/h}}$ Correct options: (A) and (C)

questionMarkup: The point where the road alignment changes from a tangent to a curve is known as ______
questionText: The point where the road alignment changes from a tangent to a curve is known as ______
explanationHtml:
In highway geometric design terminology:
The Point of Curve (PC) is the location where the tangent ends and the circular curve begins.
The Point of Tangency (PT) is where the curve ends and the tangent resumes.
The Point of Intersection (PI) is the point where two tangents intersect.
The Point of Deflection is not a standard term in horizontal curve geometry.Therefore, the point where the alignment changes from a tangent to a curve is:
Answer: (C) Point of curve
explanationText: In highway geometric design terminology:The Point of Curve (PC) is the location where the tangent ends and the circular curve begins.The Point of Tangency (PT) is where the curve ends and the tangent resumes.The Point of Intersection (PI) is the point where two tangents intersect.The Point of Deflection is not a standard term in horizontal curve geometry.Therefore, the point where the alignment changes from a tangent to a curve is: Answer: (C) Point of curve

questionText: After applying the correction for elevation and temperature, the runway length is 700 m. The corrected runway length (in m) for an effective gradient of 1% is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
explanationHtml:
Given:
Corrected runway length after elevation and temperature = 700 m 700\ \text{m} 700 m
Effective gradient = 1 1% 1
As per IRC 9157 and ICAO guidelines, if the effective gradient exceeds 0.4 0.4% 0.4, then an additional correction is applied. For an effective gradient of 1 1% 1, the recommended correction is 20% of the basic length.
So, the final corrected runway length is:
Lfinal=700+0.20×700=700×1.20=840 m L_{\text{final}} = 700 + 0.20 \times 700 = 700 \times 1.20 = 840\ \text{m} Lfinal​=700+0.20×700=700×1.20=840 m

For an effective gradient of $1%$ , the recommended correction is 20% of the basic length.So, the final corrected runway length is: $L_{\text{final}} = 700 + 0.20 \times 700 = 700 \times 1.20 = 840\ \text{m}$

questionText: The speed-density relation on a one-way, single lane road is shown in the figure, where speed $u$ is in $\mathrm{km} /$ hour and density $k$ is in vehicles/km. The maximum flow (in vehicles/hour) on this road is
explanationHtml:
The linear speed-density relationship can be written as:
u=slope⋅(k−10)+90 u = \text{slope} \cdot (k - 10) + 90 u=slope⋅(k−10)+90
slope=0−90100−10=−9090=−1 \text{slope} = \frac{0 - 90}{100 - 10} = \frac{-90}{90} = -1 slope=100−100−90​=90−90​=−1
So,
u=−1(k−10)+90=−k+100 u = -1(k - 10) + 90 = -k + 100 u=−1(k−10)+90=−k+100

Flow qqq is given by:
q=u⋅k=(100−k)⋅k=100k−k2 q = u \cdot k = (100 - k) \cdot k = 100k - k^2 q=u⋅k=(100−k)⋅k=100k−k2

To find maximum flow:
Differentiate qqq with respect to kkk:
dqdk=100−2k \frac{dq}{dk} = 100 - 2k dkdq​=100−2k
Set dqdk=0 \frac{dq}{dk} = 0 dkdq​=0:
100−2k=0⇒k=50 veh/km 100 - 2k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 50\ \text{veh/km} 100−2k=0⇒k=50 veh/km

Substitute back to find speed uuu:
u=100−50=50 km/h u = 100 - 50 = 50\ \text{km/h} u=100−50=50 km/h

Now calculate flow:
qmax=u⋅k=50⋅50=2500 veh/hr q_{\text{max}} = u \cdot k = 50 \cdot 50 = 2500\ \text{veh/hr} qmax​=u⋅k=50⋅50=2500 veh/hr
explanationText: The linear speed-density relationship can be written as: $u = \text{slope} \cdot (k - 10) + 90$ $\text{slope} = \frac{0 - 90}{100 - 10} = \frac{-90}{90} = -1$ So, $u = -1(k - 10) + 90 = -k + 100$ Flow $q$ is given by: $q = u \cdot k = (100 - k) \cdot k = 100k - k^2$ To find maximum flow: Differentiate $q$ with respect to $k$ : $\frac{dq}{dk} = 100 - 2k$ Set $\frac{dq}{dk} = 0$ : $100 - 2k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 50\ \text{veh/km}$ Substitute back to find speed $u$ : $u = 100 - 50 = 50\ \text{km/h}$ Now calculate flow: $q_{\text{max}} = u \cdot k = 50 \cdot 50 = 2500\ \text{veh/hr}$

Substitute values:
tan⁡(θ2)=92200=0.46 \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{92}{200} = 0.46 tan(2θ​)=20092​=0.46
θ2=tan⁡−1(0.46)≈24.8∘ \frac{\theta}{2} = \tan^{-1}(0.46) \approx 24.8^\circ 2θ​=tan−1(0.46)≈24.8∘
θ=2×24.8∘=49.6∘ \theta = 2 \times 24.8^\circ = \boxed{49.6^\circ} θ=2×24.8∘=49.6∘​

questionText: In the context of testing bitumen, which one of the following statements is FALSE:

options.html: The depth of penetration of needle in the standard penetration test is measured in the units of one-tenth of millimeter
options.text: The depth of penetration of needle in the standard penetration test is measured in the units of one-tenth of millimeter

options.html: Softening point is measured using a ring and ball apparatus
options.text: Softening point is measured using a ring and ball apparatus

options.html: Softening point is measured in the units of time
options.text: Softening point is measured in the units of time

options.html: Ductility is measured in the units of length
options.text: Ductility is measured in the units of length

explanationHtml:
(A) The depth of penetration of needle in the standard penetration test is measured in the units of one-tenth of millimeter.
This statement is correct. The penetration value is expressed in tenths of a millimeter.

(B) Softening point is measured using a ring and ball apparatus.
This statement is correct. The softening point test involves a steel ball and a brass ring filled with bitumen.

(C) Softening point is measured in the units of time.
This statement is false. The softening point is measured in units of temperature, typically in ∘C ^\circ \text{C} ∘C.

(D) Ductility is measured in the units of length.
This statement is correct. Ductility is usually measured in centimeters or millimeters.
explanationText: (A) The depth of penetration of needle in the standard penetration test is measured in the units of one-tenth of millimeter. This statement is correct. The penetration value is expressed in tenths of a millimeter.(B) Softening point is measured using a ring and ball apparatus. This statement is correct. The softening point test involves a steel ball and a brass ring filled with bitumen.(C) Softening point is measured in the units of time. This statement is false. The softening point is measured in units of temperature, typically in $^\circ \text{C}$ .(D) Ductility is measured in the units of length. This statement is correct. Ductility is usually measured in centimeters or millimeters.

questionText: All the vehicles that come during a particular peak hour come during a 10-minute period within this hour. The 15-minute peak hour factor for this peak hour is
explanationHtml:
Given:
All vehicles during the peak hour arrive within a 10-minute period.

To find:
15-minute Peak Hour Factor (PHF)

Formula:
PHF=Hourly Volume4×Peak 15-minute Volume\text{PHF} = \frac{\text{Hourly Volume}}{4 \times \text{Peak 15-minute Volume}}PHF=4×Peak 15-minute VolumeHourly Volume​

Since all vehicles arrive within a 10-minute period, they are included within the peak 15-minute period.

Therefore,
PHF=V4×V=14=0.25\text{PHF} = \frac{V}{4 \times V} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25PHF=4×VV​=41​=0.25

Final Answer: 0.250.250.25
explanationText: Given: All vehicles during the peak hour arrive within a 10-minute period.To find: 15-minute Peak Hour Factor (PHF)Formula: $\text{PHF} = \frac{\text{Hourly Volume}}{4 \times \text{Peak 15-minute Volume}}$ Since all vehicles arrive within a 10-minute period, they are included within the peak 15-minute period.Therefore, $\text{PHF} = \frac{V}{4 \times V} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25$ Final Answer: $0.25$

questionText: A vertical summit curve on a freight corridor is formed at the intersection of two gradients, $+3.0 \%$ and $-5.0 \%$ . explanationHtml:
Step 1: Algebraic difference of gradients
A=∣+3−(−5)∣=8 A = |+3 - (-5)| = 8% = 0.08 A=∣+3−(−5)∣=8

Step 2: Conversion of speed
V=80×10003600=22.22,m/s V = \frac{80 \times 1000}{3600} = 22.22 , \text{m/s} V=360080×1000​=22.22,m/s

Step 3: Reaction distance
Sr=V×t=22.22×2=44.44,m S_r = V \times t = 22.22 \times 2 = 44.44 , \text{m} Sr​=V×t=22.22×2=44.44,m

Step 4: Braking distance
Sb=V22gf=(22.22)22×9.81×0.36=69.94,m S_b = \frac{V^2}{2 g f} = \frac{(22.22)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.36} = 69.94 , \text{m} Sb​=2gfV2​=2×9.81×0.36(22.22)2​=69.94,m

Step 5: Stopping Sight Distance (SSD)
S=Sr+Sb=44.44+69.94=114.38,m S = S_r + S_b = 44.44 + 69.94 = 114.38 , \text{m} S=Sr​+Sb​=44.44+69.94=114.38,m

Step 6: Length of summit curve (SSD criterion)
For summit curve, when
L≥S L \ge S L≥S

L=AS22(h1+h2)2 L = \frac{A S^2}{2(\sqrt{h_1} + \sqrt{h_2})^2} L=2(h1​​+h2​​)2AS2​

h1=2.30=1.517,h2=0.35=0.592 \sqrt{h_1} = \sqrt{2.30} = 1.517, \quad \sqrt{h_2} = \sqrt{0.35} = 0.592 h1​​=2.30​=1.517,h2​​=0.35​=0.592

(h1+h2)2=(2.109)2=4.448 (\sqrt{h_1} + \sqrt{h_2})^2 = (2.109)^2 = 4.448 (h1​​+h2​​)2=(2.109)2=4.448

L=0.08×(114.38)22×4.448=1046.68.896=117.70,m L = \frac{0.08 \times (114.38)^2}{2 \times 4.448} = \frac{1046.6}{8.896} = 117.70 , \text{m} L=2×4.4480.08×(114.38)2​=8.8961046.6​=117.70,m

Check condition:
L=117.70,m≥S=114.38,m L = 117.70 , \text{m} \ge S = 114.38 , \text{m} L=117.70,m≥S=114.38,m

The number of trains and their corresponding speeds for a curved Broad Gauge section with 437 m 437 \mathrm{~m}437 m radius are

20 trains at a speed of 40 kmph
15 trains at a speed of 50 kmph
12 trains at a speed of 60 kmph
8 trains at a speed of 70 kmph
3 trains at a speed of 80 kmph

If the gauge (centre to centre distance between the rail heads) is taken as 1750 mm 1750 \mathrm{~mm}1750 mm, the required equilibrium cant (in mm\mathrm{mm}mm ) will be ____ (rounded off to the nearest integer)
questionText: The number of trains and their corresponding speeds for a curved Broad Gauge section with $437 \mathrm{~m}$ radius are 20 trains at a speed of 40 kmph 15 trains at a speed of 50 kmph 12 trains at a speed of 60 kmph 8 trains at a speed of 70 kmph 3 trains at a speed of 80 kmph If the gauge (centre to centre distance between the rail heads) is taken as $1750 \mathrm{~mm}$ , the required equilibrium cant (in $\mathrm{mm}$ ) will be ____ (rounded off to the nearest integer)
explanationText: Average speed of trains, $V_{\text {avg }}=\frac{20(40)+15(50)+12(60)+8(70)+3(80)}{20+15+12+8+3} =\frac{3070}{58} =52.93 \mathrm{kmph}$ $\text { Gauge }(G)=1750 \mathrm{~mm}$ $\therefore$ Equilibrium cant, $e_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac{G V_{\text {avg }}^{2}}{127 R}=\frac{1750 \times(52.93)^{2}}{127 \times 437}=88.34 =88 \mathrm{~mm}$

questionMarkup: As per the Indian Roads Congress guidelines (IRC 86: 2018), extra widening depends on which of the following parameters?
questionText: As per the Indian Roads Congress guidelines (IRC 86: 2018), extra widening depends on which of the following parameters?
explanationHtml:
As per IRC 86:201886: 201886:2018 Clause 8.6 Widening of Carriageway on Curves:
At sharp horizontal curves, it is necessary to widen the carriageway to provide for safe passage of vehicles. The widening required has two components: (i) mechanical widening to components for the extra width occupied by a vehicle on the curve due to tracking of the rare wheels, and (ii) psychological widening to permit easy crossing of vehicles since vehicles in a lane tend to wander more on a curve than on a straight reach.
On two-lane or wider roads, it is necessary that both the above components should be fully catered for so that the lateral clearance between vehicles of curves is maintained equal to the clearance available on straight. Position of single-lane roads however is somewhat different.
Since during crossing maneuvers outer wheels of vehicles have in any case to use the shoulder whether on the straight or on the curve. It is, therefore sufficient on single lane roads if only the mechanical component of widening is taken into account.
Based on the above considerations, the extra width of carriageway to be provided at horizontal curves on single and two-lane roads is given in Table For multi-lane roads, the pavement widening may be calculated by adding half the widening for two-lane roads to each lane.
Table : Extra width of Pavement at Horizontal Curves

If the allowable jerk is $0.75 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{3}$ , what is the minimum length (in $\mathrm{m}$ , in integer) of the transition curve ?
explanationText: Radius of circular curve $(\mathrm{R})=300 \mathrm{~m}$ $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Allowable jerk $(\mathrm{C})=0.75 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}^{3}$ $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{L}_{\min }=\frac{\mathrm{v}^{3}}{\mathrm{CR}} \\ & \mathrm{L}_{\min }=\frac{(15)^{3}}{0.75 \times(300)}=15 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore \quad$ Minimum length of transition curve $=15 \mathrm{~m}$ .

questionText: The lane configuration with lane volumes in vehicles per hour of a four-arm signalized intersection is shown in the figure. There are only two phases: the first phase is for the East-West and the West-East through movements, and the second phase is for the North-South and the South-North through movements. There are no turning movements. Assume that the saturation flow is 1800 vehicles per hour per lane for each lane and the total lost time for the first and the second phases together is 9 seconds.The optimum cycle length (in seconds), as per the Webster's method, is ____________. (round off to the nearest integer)

explanationHtml:
Correction for elevation = It should increase at a rate of 7% per 300 m rise in elevation from MSL.
Given that
Basic runway length as MSL =1500m

Correction =7100×300300×1500=105m =\frac{7}{100}\times \frac{300}{300}\times 1500=105m=1007​×300300​×1500=105m
The actual length of runway= 1500+150=1605m

explanationHtml: λC=4  vehical/hr=2  vehical/30  minλC=2  vehical/hr=1  vehical/30  minλVehical=3  vehical/30  minP(x<2)=1−P(x≤1)=1−[P(x=0)+P(x=1)]=1−[e−λλ00!+e−λλ11!]=1−e−3(1+3)=1−4e3=0.8\begin{aligned} \lambda _C&=4 \; vehical/hr=2 \; vehical /30 \;min\\ \lambda _C&=2 \; vehical/hr=1 \; vehical /30 \;min\\ \lambda _{Vehical}&=3 \; vehical/30 \;min\\ P(x \lt 2)&=1-P(x\leq 1)\\ &=1-[P(x=0)+P(x=1)]\\ &=1-\left [ \frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^0}{0!} +\frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^1}{1!}\right ]\\ &=1-e^{-3}(1+3)\\ &=1-\frac{4}{e^3}\\ &=0.8 \end{aligned} λC​λC​λVehical​P(x<2)​=4vehical/hr=2vehical/30min=2vehical/hr=1vehical/30min=3vehical/30min=1−P(x≤1)=1−[P(x=0)+P(x=1)]=1−[0!e−λλ0​+1!e−λλ1​]=1−e−3(1+3)=1−e34​=0.8​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \lambda _C&=4 \; vehical/hr=2 \; vehical /30 \;min\\ \lambda _C&=2 \; vehical/hr=1 \; vehical /30 \;min\\ \lambda _{Vehical}&=3 \; vehical/30 \;min\\ P(x \lt 2)&=1-P(x\leq 1)\\ &=1-[P(x=0)+P(x=1)]\\ &=1-\left [ \frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^0}{0!} +\frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^1}{1!}\right ]\\ &=1-e^{-3}(1+3)\\ &=1-\frac{4}{e^3}\\ &=0.8 \end{aligned}$
explanationTex:
\begin{aligned}
\lambda _C&=4 \; vehical/hr=2 \; vehical /30 \;min\\
\lambda _C&=2 \; vehical/hr=1 \; vehical /30 \;min\\
\lambda _{Vehical}&=3 \; vehical/30 \;min\\
P(x \lt  2)&=1-P(x\leq 1)\\

lost time per phase due to start-up and clearance is 2 s, the effective green time
of each phase is ______s. (in integer)
questionText: A two-phase signalized intersection is designed with a cycle time of 100 s. The amber and red times for each phase are 4 s and 50 s, respectively. If the total lost time per phase due to start-up and clearance is 2 s, the effective green time of each phase is ______s. (in integer)
explanationHtml:
Two phase signalized intersections,
Cycle time = 100 secs.
Amber time = 4 secs. [each phase]
Red time = 50 secs. [each phase]
Total lost time = 2 sec. [each phase]
Effective green time = ? [each phase]
Total Effective green = Cycle time - Lost time = 100-2x2 = 96 sec.
As there is symmetry in phases so effective green time per phase= 96/2=48 sec.
explanationText: Two phase signalized intersections, Cycle time = 100 secs. Amber time = 4 secs. [each phase] Red time = 50 secs. [each phase] Total lost time = 2 sec. [each phase] Effective green time = ? [each phase] Total Effective green = Cycle time - Lost time = 100-2x2 = 96 sec. As there is symmetry in phases so effective green time per phase= 96/2=48 sec.

questionText: In a three-phase signal system design for a four-leg intersection, the critical flow ratios for each phase are 0.18, 0.32, and 0.22. The total loss time in each of the phases is 2s. As per Webster's formula, the optimal cycle length (in s, round off to the nearest integer) is _______________
explanationHtml: L=2×3=6 seconds n=3y=(0.18+0.32+0.22)C0=(1.5L+51−y)=(1.5×6+51−(0.18+0.32+0.22))=50 seconds \begin{aligned} L &=2 \times 3=6 \text { seconds } \\ n &=3 \\ y &=(0.18+0.32+0.22) \\ C_{0} &=\left(\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y}\right)=\left(\frac{1.5 \times 6+5}{1-(0.18+0.32+0.22)}\right) \\ &=50 \text { seconds } \end{aligned}LnyC0​​=2×3=6 seconds =3=(0.18+0.32+0.22)=(1−y1.5L+5​)=(1−(0.18+0.32+0.22)1.5×6+5​)=50 seconds ​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} L &=2 \times 3=6 \text { seconds } \\ n &=3 \\ y &=(0.18+0.32+0.22) \\ C_{0} &=\left(\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y}\right)=\left(\frac{1.5 \times 6+5}{1-(0.18+0.32+0.22)}\right) \\ &=50 \text { seconds } \end{aligned}$

questionMarkup: Vehicular arrival at an isolated intersection follows the Poisson distribution. The mean vehicular arrival rate is 2 vehicle per minute. The probability (round off to two decimal places) that at least 2 vehicles will arrive in any given 1-minute interval is _____
questionText: Vehicular arrival at an isolated intersection follows the Poisson distribution. The mean vehicular arrival rate is 2 vehicle per minute. The probability (round off to two decimal places) that at least 2 vehicles will arrive in any given 1-minute interval is _____
explanationHtml:
P(n,t)=(λt)ne−λtn!P(n,t)=\frac{(\lambda t)^n e^{-\lambda t}}{n!}P(n,t)=n!(λt)ne−λt​
λ=2  v/m\lambda =2 \;v/mλ=2v/m
t=1 minutet = 1 \text{ minute}t=1 minute
probability of at least 2 vehicles arriving in 1 ? minute is given by,
1−(P(0,1)+P(1,1))1-(P(0,1)+P(1,1))1−(P(0,1)+P(1,1))
=1−{(2×1)0e−2(1)0!+(2×1)1e−2(1)1!}=1−{1(e−2)1+2(e−2)1}=1−(e−2+2e−2)=1−3e−2=0.59\begin{aligned} &= 1-\left \{ \frac{(2 \times 1)^0 e^{-2(1)}}{0!}+\frac{(2 \times 1)^1 e^{-2(1)}}{1!} \right \}\\ &=1-\left \{ \frac{1(e^{-2})}{1}+ \frac{2(e^{-2})}{1} \right \} \\ &= 1-(e^{-2}+2e^{-2})\\ &=1-3e^{-2}=0.59 \end{aligned}​=1−{0!(2×1)0e−2(1)​+1!(2×1)1e−2(1)​}=1−{11(e−2)​+12(e−2)​}=1−(e−2+2e−2)=1−3e−2=0.59​
explanationText: $P(n,t)=\frac{(\lambda t)^n e^{-\lambda t}}{n!}$ $\lambda =2 \;v/m$ $t = 1 \text{ minute}$ probability of at least 2 vehicles arriving in 1 ? minute is given by, $1-(P(0,1)+P(1,1))$ $\begin{aligned} &= 1-\left \{ \frac{(2 \times 1)^0 e^{-2(1)}}{0!}+\frac{(2 \times 1)^1 e^{-2(1)}}{1!} \right \}\\ &=1-\left \{ \frac{1(e^{-2})}{1}+ \frac{2(e^{-2})}{1} \right \} \\ &= 1-(e^{-2}+2e^{-2})\\ &=1-3e^{-2}=0.59 \end{aligned}$

questionText: A signalized intersection operates in two phases. The lost time is 3 seconds per phase. The maximum ratios of approach flow to saturation flow for the two phases are 0.37 and 0.40. The optimum cycle length using the Webster's method (in seconds, round off to one decimal place) is ______________
explanationHtml: n=2, L=3×2=6secy1=0.37,y2=0.40Y=y1+y2=0.37+0.40=0.77C0=(1.5 L+51−Y)=1.5×6+51−0.77=60.87sec≃60.9sec\begin{aligned} \mathrm{n} &=2, \mathrm{~L}=3 \times 2=6 \mathrm{sec} \\ \mathrm{y}_{1} &=0.37, \mathrm{y}_{2}=0.40 \\ \mathrm{Y} &=\mathrm{y}_{1}+\mathrm{y}_{2} \\ &=0.37+0.40 \\ &=0.77 \\ \mathrm{C}_{0} &=\left(\frac{1.5 \mathrm{~L}+5}{1-\mathrm{Y}}\right)=\frac{1.5 \times 6+5}{1-0.77} \\ &=60.87 \mathrm{sec} \simeq 60.9 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}ny1​YC0​​=2, L=3×2=6sec=0.37,y2​=0.40=y1​+y2​=0.37+0.40=0.77=(1−Y1.5 L+5​)=1−0.771.5×6+5​=60.87sec≃60.9sec​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{n} &=2, \mathrm{~L}=3 \times 2=6 \mathrm{sec} \\ \mathrm{y}_{1} &=0.37, \mathrm{y}_{2}=0.40 \\ \mathrm{Y} &=\mathrm{y}_{1}+\mathrm{y}_{2} \\ &=0.37+0.40 \\ &=0.77 \\ \mathrm{C}_{0} &=\left(\frac{1.5 \mathrm{~L}+5}{1-\mathrm{Y}}\right)=\frac{1.5 \times 6+5}{1-0.77} \\ &=60.87 \mathrm{sec} \simeq 60.9 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}$

questionText: 24-h traffic count at a road section was observed to be 1000 vehicles on a Tuesday in the month of July. If daily adjustment factor for Tuesday is 1.121 and monthly adjustment factor for July is 0.913, the Annual Average Daily Traffic (in veh/day, round off to the nearest integer) is _______.

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} T_{24} &=1000 veh \; (Tuesday) \\ DAF&=1.121 \\ AADT&=? \\ MAF&= 0.913\\ T_{week}&=T_{24} \times DAF \\ &=1000 \times 1.121=1121 \\ AADT&=MAF \times ADT \\ &= 0.913 \times 1121\\ &= 1023.473\\ &=1023 VPD \end{aligned}$

questionText: A vehicle is moving on a road of grade +4% at a speed of 20 m/s. Consider the coefficient of rolling friction as 0.46 and acceleration due to gravity as 10 $m/s^2$ . On applying brakes to reach a speed of 10 m/s, the required braking distance (in m, round off to nearest integer) along the horizontal, is ______
explanationHtml:
Given,
Upward gradient, G = 4% = 0.04 (upgrade is taken as +ve)
Initial speed, v1v_1v1​ = 20 m/s
Coefficient of friction (rolling), f = 0.46
Acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m/s2m/s^2m/s2
Final velocity due to break application (reduced), v2v_2v2​ = 10 m/s
Breaking distance,
Sb=(v12−v22)2g(f+G)=(202−102)2×10(0.46+0.04)=30m\begin{aligned} S_b&=\frac{(v_1^2-v_2^2)}{2g(f+G)} \\ &=\frac{(20^2-10^2)}{2 \times 10(0.46+0.04)} \\ &= 30m \end{aligned}Sb​​=2g(f+G)(v12​−v22​)​=2×10(0.46+0.04)(202−102)​=30m​
explanationText: Given, Upward gradient, G = 4% = 0.04 (upgrade is taken as +ve) Initial speed, $v_1$ = 20 m/s Coefficient of friction (rolling), f = 0.46 Acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 $m/s^2$ Final velocity due to break application (reduced), $v_2$ = 10 m/sBreaking distance, $\begin{aligned} S_b&=\frac{(v_1^2-v_2^2)}{2g(f+G)} \\ &=\frac{(20^2-10^2)}{2 \times 10(0.46+0.04)} \\ &= 30m \end{aligned}$

questionText: The maximum number of vehicles observed in any five minute period during the peak hour is 160. If the total flow in the peak hour is 1000 vehicles, the five minute peak hour factor (round off to 2 decimal places) is ___
explanationHtml:
Given actual flow in peak hour, qactual=103  veh/hrq_{actual}=10^3 \;\text{veh/hr}qactual​=103veh/hr
peak 5 min rate = 160 veh/5min
Peak (5min)rate volume, qpeak rate=160560=1920  veh/hrq_{\text{peak rate}}=\frac{160}{\frac{5}{60}} =1920\;\text{veh/hr}qpeak rate​=605​160​=1920veh/hr
Therefore, peak hourly factor (PHF) for 5 min is
PHF5=qactualqpeak rate=1031920=0.52083≈0.52PHF_5=\frac{q_{\text{actual}}}{q_{\text{peak rate}}}=\frac{10^3}{1920}=0.52083\approx 0.52PHF5​=qpeak rate​qactual​​=1920103​=0.52083≈0.52
explanationText: Given actual flow in peak hour, $q_{actual}=10^3 \;\text{veh/hr}$ peak 5 min rate = 160 veh/5min Peak (5min)rate volume, $q_{\text{peak rate}}=\frac{160}{\frac{5}{60}} =1920\;\text{veh/hr}$ Therefore, peak hourly factor (PHF) for 5 min is $PHF_5=\frac{q_{\text{actual}}}{q_{\text{peak rate}}}=\frac{10^3}{1920}=0.52083\approx 0.52$

explanationHtml:
SSD2=0.278×VtR+V2254f=0.278×50×2.5+502254×0.38≃61mSSD1=0.278×20×2.5+202254×0.38≃18m\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SSD}_{2} &=0.278 \times V t_{R}+\frac{V^{2}}{254 f} \\ &=0.278 \times 50 \times 2.5+\frac{50^{2}}{254 \times 0.38} \simeq 61 \mathrm{m} \\ \mathrm{SSD}_{1} &=0.278 \times 20 \times 2.5+\frac{20^{2}}{254 \times 0.38} \simeq 18 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}SSD2​SSD1​​=0.278×VtR​+254fV2​=0.278×50×2.5+254×0.38502​≃61m=0.278×20×2.5+254×0.38202​≃18m​
As per data given and based on calculation of SSD the answer would be 61 m and 18 m.
But, as per the code IRC : 66 of sight distance calculation at priority intersection, the sight triangle at priority intersection should be formed by measuring a distance of 15 m along minor road and a distance equal to 8 seconds travel at the design speed (50×0.278×8≃111m)(50 \times 0.278 \times 8 \simeq 111 m) (50×0.278×8≃111m) along major road. Hence answer will be 111 m and 15 m.
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SSD}_{2} &=0.278 \times V t_{R}+\frac{V^{2}}{254 f} \\ &=0.278 \times 50 \times 2.5+\frac{50^{2}}{254 \times 0.38} \simeq 61 \mathrm{m} \\ \mathrm{SSD}_{1} &=0.278 \times 20 \times 2.5+\frac{20^{2}}{254 \times 0.38} \simeq 18 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$ As per data given and based on calculation of SSD the answer would be 61 m and 18 m. But, as per the code IRC : 66 of sight distance calculation at priority intersection, the sight triangle at priority intersection should be formed by measuring a distance of 15 m along minor road and a distance equal to 8 seconds travel at the design speed $(50 \times 0.278 \times 8 \simeq 111 m)$ along major road. Hence answer will be 111 m and 15 m.

explanationText: Sliding occurs if $\begin{aligned} f& \lt e\\ \text{and }\quad f& \lt \frac{V^{2}}{g R} \end{aligned}$ Overturning occurs if $\begin{aligned} f& \gt e\\ \text{and }\quad e& \lt \frac{V^{2}}{g R} \end{aligned}$ Hence, option (A) is true.

questionText: In Marshall method of mix design, the coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, fines and bitumen having respective values of specific gravity 2.60, 2.70, 2.65 and 1.01, are mixed in the relative proportions (% by weight) of 55.0, 35.8, 3.7 and 5.5 respectively. explanationHtml:
Theoretical specific gravity,
Gt=w1+w2+w3+w4w1G1+W2G2+W3G3+W4Gb=55+35.8+3.7+5.5552.6+35.82.7+3.72.65+5.51.01+=2.42 \begin{aligned} G_{t} &=\frac{w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3}+w_{4}}{\frac{w_{1}}{G_{1}}+\frac{W_{2}}{G_{2}}+\frac{W_{3}}{G_{3}}+\frac{W_{4}}{G_{b}}} \\ &=\frac{55+35.8+3.7+5.5}{\frac{55}{2.6}+\frac{35.8}{2.7}+\frac{3.7}{2.65}+\frac{5.5}{1.01}}+ \\ &=2.42 \end{aligned}Gt​​=G1​w1​​+G2​W2​​+G3​W3​​+Gb​W4​​w1​+w2​+w3​+w4​​=2.655​+2.735.8​+2.653.7​+1.015.5​55+35.8+3.7+5.5​+=2.42​

G′=(55×2.6)+(35.8×2.7)55+35.8=2.639=2.64 \begin{aligned} G^{\prime} &=\frac{(55 \times 2.6)+(35.8 \times 2.7)}{55+35.8} \\ &=2.639=2.64 \end{aligned}G′​=55+35.8(55×2.6)+(35.8×2.7)​=2.639=2.64​
explanationText: Theoretical specific gravity, $\begin{aligned} G_{t} &=\frac{w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3}+w_{4}}{\frac{w_{1}}{G_{1}}+\frac{W_{2}}{G_{2}}+\frac{W_{3}}{G_{3}}+\frac{W_{4}}{G_{b}}} \\ &=\frac{55+35.8+3.7+5.5}{\frac{55}{2.6}+\frac{35.8}{2.7}+\frac{3.7}{2.65}+\frac{5.5}{1.01}}+ \\ &=2.42 \end{aligned}$ Effective specific gravity of aggregates (coarse + fine) is given by, $\begin{aligned} G^{\prime} &=\frac{(55 \times 2.6)+(35.8 \times 2.7)}{55+35.8} \\ &=2.639=2.64 \end{aligned}$

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} &\frac{d v}{d t}=\alpha-\beta v\\ &\Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{d v}{(\alpha-\beta v)}=\int d t\\ &\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\ln (\alpha-\beta v)}{-\beta}=t+C\\ &\text { at } t=3 \text { sec, } \frac{d v}{d t}=\alpha-\beta v=1.3 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\\ &\Rightarrow \frac{\ln (1.3)}{-0.05}=3+c \Rightarrow c=-8.247\\ &\therefore \quad \ln (2-0.05 \times v)=(t-8.247)(-0.05)\\ &\Rightarrow 2-0.05 \times v=1.51 \mathrm{e}^{-0.05 t}\\ &\Rightarrow v=\frac{d s}{d t}=40-30.21 e^{-0.05 t}\\ &\Rightarrow s=40 t+604.15 e^{-0.05 t}+c^{\prime}\\ &\therefore \quad \text { at } t=0, s=0 \Rightarrow c^{\prime}=-604.15\\ &\Rightarrow \quad s=40 t+604.15 e^{-0.05 t}-604.15\\ &\text { at } t=35 \mathrm{sec}\\ &\Rightarrow \quad s=40 \times 35+604.15 \mathrm{e}^{-0.05 \times 35}-604\\ &\Rightarrow \quad s=900.84 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned} &\frac{d v}{d t}=\alpha-\beta v\\ &\Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{d v}{(\alpha-\beta v)}=\int d t\\ &\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\ln (\alpha-\beta v)}{-\beta}=t+C\\ &\text { at } t=3 \text { sec, } \frac{d v}{d t}=\alpha-\beta v=1.3 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\\ &\Rightarrow \frac{\ln (1.3)}{-0.05}=3+c \Rightarrow c=-8.247\\ &\therefore \quad \ln (2-0.05 \times v)=(t-8.247)(-0.05)\\ &\Rightarrow 2-0.05 \times v=1.51 \mathrm{e}^{-0.05 t}\\ &\Rightarrow v=\frac{d s}{d t}=40-30.21 e^{-0.05 t}\\ &\Rightarrow s=40 t+604.15 e^{-0.05 t}+c^{\prime}\\ &\therefore \quad \text { at } t=0, s=0 \Rightarrow c^{\prime}=-604.15\\ &\Rightarrow \quad s=40 t+604.15 e^{-0.05 t}-604.15\\ &\text { at } t=35 \mathrm{sec}\\ &\Rightarrow \quad s=40 \times 35+604.15 \mathrm{e}^{-0.05 \times 35}-604\\ &\Rightarrow \quad s=900.84 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}

questionMarkup: The penetration value of a bitumen sample tested at 25∘^{\circ}∘C is 80. When this sample is heated to 60∘^{\circ}∘C and tested again, the needle of the penetration test apparatus penetrates the bitumen sample by d mm. The value of d CANNOT be less than _____mm.
questionText: The penetration value of a bitumen sample tested at 25 $^{\circ}$ C is 80. When this sample is heated to 60 $^{\circ}$ C and tested again, the needle of the penetration test apparatus penetrates the bitumen sample by d mm. The value of d CANNOT be less than _____mm.
explanationHtml:
Relationship between penetration and temperature
is given by,
P=AT+KP= Penetration A=Temperature susceptibility K=Constant  \begin{array}{l} P=A T+K \\ P=\text { Penetration }\\ A= \text{Temperature susceptibility }\\ K= \text{Constant }\\ \end{array}P=AT+KP= Penetration A=Temperature susceptibility K=Constant ​
With increase in temperature, penetration
increases.
Hence, we will simply take,
d≮8010=8mm d \nless \frac{80}{10}=8 \mathrm{mm}d≮1080​=8mm
explanationText: Relationship between penetration and temperature is given by, $\begin{array}{l} P=A T+K \\ P=\text { Penetration }\\ A= \text{Temperature susceptibility }\\ K= \text{Constant }\\ \end{array}$ With increase in temperature, penetration increases. Hence, we will simply take, $d \nless \frac{80}{10}=8 \mathrm{mm}$
explanationTex: \begin{array}{l} P=A T+K \\ P=\text { Penetration }\\ A= \text{Temperature susceptibility }\\ K= \text{Constant }\\ \end{array}

questionText: A pre-timed four phase signal has critical lane flow rate for the first three phases as 200, 187 and 210 veh/hr with saturation flow rate of 1800 veh/hr/lane for all phases. The lost time is given as 4 seconds for each phase. If the cycle length is 60 seconds, the effective green time (in seconds) of the fourth phase is _________
explanationHtml:
Flow rates for the first three phase are given as
q1=200veh/hrq2=187veh/hrandq3=210 veh/hr  \begin{aligned} q_{1}&=200 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \\ q_{2}&=187 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr}\\ \text{and}\quad q_{3}&=210 \text { veh/hr } \end{aligned}q1​q2​andq3​​=200veh/hr=187veh/hr=210 veh/hr ​
Saturation flow rate is 1800 veh/hr/lane
Lost time,
L=4×4=16sec L=4 \times 4=16 \mathrm{sec}L=4×4=16sec
Length of the cycle,
C0=60sec C_{0}=60 \mathrm{sec}C0​=60sec
 Now, y1=q1s1=2001800y2=q2s2=1871800y3=q3s3=2101800C0=1.5L+51−y⇒60=1.5×16+51−y⇒60=24+51−y⇒1−y=2960⇒y=1−2960=60−2960=0.517Andy=y1+y2+y3+y4⇒0.517=5971800+y4⇒y4=0.185G=y4y(C0−L)=0.1850.517(60−16)=15.745sec \begin{aligned} \text { Now, } \quad y_{1} &=\frac{q_{1}}{s_{1}}=\frac{200}{1800} \\ y_{2} &=\frac{q_{2}}{s_{2}}=\frac{187}{1800} \\ y_{3} &=\frac{q_{3}}{s_{3}}=\frac{210}{1800} \\ C_{0} &=\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 60 &=\frac{1.5 \times 16+5}{1-y}\\ \Rightarrow 60 &=\frac{24+5}{1-y} \\ \Rightarrow 1-y &=\frac{29}{60} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=\frac{1-29}{60}=\frac{60-29}{60} \\ &=0.517\\ \text{And}\quad y&=y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}+y_{4}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.517 &=\frac{597}{1800}+y_{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{4}&=0.185 \\ G &=\frac{y_{4}}{y}\left(C_{0}-L\right)\\ &=\frac{0.185}{0.517}(60-16) \\ &=15.745 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} Now, y1​y2​y3​C0​⇒60⇒60⇒1−y⇒yAndy⇒0.517⇒y4​G​=s1​q1​​=1800200​=s2​q2​​=1800187​=s3​q3​​=1800210​=1−y1.5L+5​=1−y1.5×16+5​=1−y24+5​=6029​=601−29​=6060−29​=0.517=y1​+y2​+y3​+y4​=1800597​+y4​=0.185=yy4​​(C0​−L)=0.5170.185​(60−16)=15.745sec​
explanationText: Flow rates for the first three phase are given as $\begin{aligned} q_{1}&=200 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \\ q_{2}&=187 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr}\\ \text{and}\quad q_{3}&=210 \text { veh/hr } \end{aligned}$ Saturation flow rate is 1800 veh/hr/lane Lost time, $L=4 \times 4=16 \mathrm{sec}$ Length of the cycle, $C_{0}=60 \mathrm{sec}$ $\begin{aligned} \text { Now, } \quad y_{1} &=\frac{q_{1}}{s_{1}}=\frac{200}{1800} \\ y_{2} &=\frac{q_{2}}{s_{2}}=\frac{187}{1800} \\ y_{3} &=\frac{q_{3}}{s_{3}}=\frac{210}{1800} \\ C_{0} &=\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 60 &=\frac{1.5 \times 16+5}{1-y}\\ \Rightarrow 60 &=\frac{24+5}{1-y} \\ \Rightarrow 1-y &=\frac{29}{60} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=\frac{1-29}{60}=\frac{60-29}{60} \\ &=0.517\\ \text{And}\quad y&=y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}+y_{4}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.517 &=\frac{597}{1800}+y_{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{4}&=0.185 \\ G &=\frac{y_{4}}{y}\left(C_{0}-L\right)\\ &=\frac{0.185}{0.517}(60-16) \\ &=15.745 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}$

v=80−2k3Capacity,=v×k=80k−2k23\begin{aligned} v&=80-\frac{2 k}{3} \\ \text{Capacity,}\quad &=v \times k \\ &=80 k-\frac{2 k^{2}}{3} \end{aligned}vCapacity,​=80−32k​=v×k=80k−32k2​​

dqdk=0⇒dqdk=80−4k3=0⇒k=60 \begin{aligned} \frac{d q}{d k}&=0\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d q}{d k} &=80-\frac{4 k}{3}=0 \\ \Rightarrow k&=60 \end{aligned} dkdq​⇒dkdq​⇒k​=0=80−34k​=0=60​

questionText: In a Marshall sample, the bulk specific gravity of mix and aggregates are 2.324 and 2.546 respectively. The sample includes 5% of bitumen (by total weight of mix) of specific gravity 1.10. The theoretical maximum specific gravity of mix is 2.441. The void filled with bitumen (VFB) in the Marshall sample (in %) is _______
explanationHtml:
Vv=Gt−GmGt×100=2.441−2.3242.441×100V_{v}=\frac{G_{t}-G_{m}}{G_{t}} \times 100=\frac{2.441-2.324}{2.441} \times 100Vv​=Gt​Gt​−Gm​​×100=2.4412.441−2.324​×100
=4.79% =4.79 \% =4.79%
Void filled with bitumen,
Vb=Gm×Wb(%)Gb=2.324×51.1=10.56%VMA=Vv+Vb=4.79+10.56=15.35%∴VFB=Vb(%)VMA×100=10.5615.35×100=68.79% \begin{array}{l} V_{b}=G_{m} \times \frac{W_{b}(\%)}{G_{b}}=2.324 \times \frac{5}{1.1}=10.56 \%\\ \mathrm{VMA}=V_{v}+V_{b}=4.79+10.56=15.35 \% \\ \therefore \mathrm{VFB}=\frac{V_{b}(\%)}{\mathrm{VMA}} \times 100=\frac{10.56}{15.35} \times 100=68.79 \% \end{array}Vb​=Gm​×Gb​Wb​(%)​=2.324×1.15​=10.56%VMA=Vv​+Vb​=4.79+10.56=15.35%∴VFB=VMAVb​(%)​×100=15.3510.56​×100=68.79%​
explanationText: $V_{v}=\frac{G_{t}-G_{m}}{G_{t}} \times 100=\frac{2.441-2.324}{2.441} \times 100$ $=4.79 \%$ Void filled with bitumen, $\begin{array}{l} V_{b}=G_{m} \times \frac{W_{b}(\%)}{G_{b}}=2.324 \times \frac{5}{1.1}=10.56 \%\\ \mathrm{VMA}=V_{v}+V_{b}=4.79+10.56=15.35 \% \\ \therefore \mathrm{VFB}=\frac{V_{b}(\%)}{\mathrm{VMA}} \times 100=\frac{10.56}{15.35} \times 100=68.79 \% \end{array}$

questionText: An isolated three-phase traffic signal is designed by Webster's method. The critical flow ratios for three phases are 0.20, 0.30, and 0.25 respectively, and lost time per phase is 4 seconds. The optimum cycle length (in seconds) is ___________
explanationHtml:
Sum of the flow,
y=y1+y2+y3=0.2+0.3+0.25=0.75 \begin{aligned} y &=y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3} \\ &=0.2+0.3+0.25=0.75 \end{aligned}y​=y1​+y2​+y3​=0.2+0.3+0.25=0.75​
Total lost time in a cycle L=4×3=12 sec.L=4 \times 3=12\text{ sec}. L=4×3=12 sec.
Optimum cycle length,
C0=1.5L+51−y1.5×12+51−0.75=92sec \begin{aligned} C_{0} &=\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y} \\ \frac{1.5 \times 12+5}{1-0.75} &=92 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}C0​1−0.751.5×12+5​​=1−y1.5L+5​=92sec​
explanationText: Sum of the flow, $\begin{aligned} y &=y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3} \\ &=0.2+0.3+0.25=0.75 \end{aligned}$ Total lost time in a cycle $L=4 \times 3=12\text{ sec}.$ Optimum cycle length, $\begin{aligned} C_{0} &=\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y} \\ \frac{1.5 \times 12+5}{1-0.75} &=92 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}$

questionMarkup: The speed-density (u-k) relationship on a single lane road with unidirectional flow u= 70-0.7k, where u is in km/hr and k is in veh/km. The capacity of the road (in veh/hr) is________
questionText: The speed-density (u-k) relationship on a single lane road with unidirectional flow u= 70-0.7k, where u is in km/hr and k is in veh/km. The capacity of the road (in veh/hr) is________
explanationHtml: Capacity = Velocity × Density ⇒C=V×K=70K−0.7K2 Now, dCdK=70−1.4K=0⇒K=50⇒ Capacity, =70×50−0.7(50)2=1750veh/hr\begin{aligned} \text { Capacity } &=\text { Velocity } \times \text { Density } \\ \Rightarrow \quad C &=V \times K \\ &=70 K-0.7 K^{2} \\ \text { Now, } \quad \frac{d C}{d K} &=70-1.4 K=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K &=50\\ \Rightarrow \quad \text { Capacity, } &=70 \times 50-0.7(50)^{2} \\ &=1750 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \end{aligned} Capacity ⇒C Now, dKdC​⇒K⇒ Capacity, ​= Velocity × Density =V×K=70K−0.7K2=70−1.4K=0=50=70×50−0.7(50)2=1750veh/hr​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \text { Capacity } &=\text { Velocity } \times \text { Density } \\ \Rightarrow \quad C &=V \times K \\ &=70 K-0.7 K^{2} \\ \text { Now, } \quad \frac{d C}{d K} &=70-1.4 K=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K &=50\\ \Rightarrow \quad \text { Capacity, } &=70 \times 50-0.7(50)^{2} \\ &=1750 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned} \text { Capacity } &=\text { Velocity } \times \text { Density } \\ \Rightarrow \quad C &=V \times K \\ &=70 K-0.7 K^{2} \\ \text { Now, } \quad \frac{d C}{d K} &=70-1.4 K=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K &=50\\ \Rightarrow \quad \text { Capacity, } &=70 \times 50-0.7(50)^{2} \\ &=1750 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \end{aligned}

questionText: The perception-reaction time for a vehicle travelling at 90 km/h, given the coefficient of longitudinal friction of 0.35 and the stopping sight distance of 170 m (assume g = 9.81 $m/s^{2}$ ), is _____________ seconds.
explanationHtml: SSD=0.278vtr+(0.278v)22gf⇒170=0.278×90×tr+(0.278×90)22×9.81×0.35⇒tr=3.1510sec\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SSD}&=0.278 \mathrm{vt}_{r}+\frac{(0.278 \mathrm{v})^{2}}{2 \mathrm{gf}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 170&=0.278 \times 90 \times t_{r}+\frac{(0.278 \times 90)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.35} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad t_{r}&=3.1510 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}SSD⇒170⇒tr​​=0.278vtr​+2gf(0.278v)2​=0.278×90×tr​+2×9.81×0.35(0.278×90)2​=3.1510sec​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SSD}&=0.278 \mathrm{vt}_{r}+\frac{(0.278 \mathrm{v})^{2}}{2 \mathrm{gf}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 170&=0.278 \times 90 \times t_{r}+\frac{(0.278 \times 90)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.35} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad t_{r}&=3.1510 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}$

questionText: It was observed that 150 vehicles crossed a particular location of a highway ina duration of 30 minutes. Assuming that vehicle arrival follows a negative exponential distribution, find out the number of time headways greater than 5 seconds in the above observation? __________
explanationHtml:
P(x)=λne−λx!P(x)=\frac{\lambda^{n} e^{-\lambda}}{x !}P(x)=x!λne−λ​
Where, P(x) is the probability of x events (vehicle arrivals) in some time interval (t).
λ \lambda λ is the mean arrival rate in that interval.
λ=15030×60×5=512 \lambda=\frac{150}{30 \times 60} \times 5=\frac{5}{12}λ=30×60150​×5=125​
Now, the probability that zero vehicle arrive in an interval t, denoted as P(0), will be same as the probability that the headway (into arrival time) greater than or equal to t.
∴P(x=0)=λ0e−λ0!=e−5/12=0.6592∴P(x=0)=0.6592 \begin{array}{l} \therefore P(x=0)=\frac{\lambda^{0} e^{-\lambda}}{0 !}=e^{-5 / 12}=0.6592 \\ \therefore P(x=0)=0.6592 \end{array}∴P(x=0)=0!λ0e−λ​=e−5/12=0.6592∴P(x=0)=0.6592​
Number of time headway in 30 minutes
=0.6592×30×60=1186.63 \begin{array}{l} =0.6592 \times 30 \times 60 \\ =1186.63 \end{array}=0.6592×30×60=1186.63​
explanationText: $P(x)=\frac{\lambda^{n} e^{-\lambda}}{x !}$ Where, P(x) is the probability of x events (vehicle arrivals) in some time interval (t). $\lambda$ is the mean arrival rate in that interval. $\lambda=\frac{150}{30 \times 60} \times 5=\frac{5}{12}$ Now, the probability that zero vehicle arrive in an interval t, denoted as P(0), will be same as the probability that the headway (into arrival time) greater than or equal to t. $\begin{array}{l} \therefore P(x=0)=\frac{\lambda^{0} e^{-\lambda}}{0 !}=e^{-5 / 12}=0.6592 \\ \therefore P(x=0)=0.6592 \end{array}$ Number of time headway in 30 minutes $\begin{array}{l} =0.6592 \times 30 \times 60 \\ =1186.63 \end{array}$

options.html: I is true, II is false

options.html: I is true, II is true, and II is the correct reason for I
options.text: I is true, II is true, and II is the correct reason for I

options.text: I is true, II is true, and II is NOT the correct reason for I

options.html: I is false, II is true
options.text: I is false, II is true

explanationHtml:
When fast moving vehicle travels along a summit curve the centrifugal force will act upwards against gravity and hence a part of the pressure on the tyres and spring of the vehicle suspensions is relieved. So there is no problem of discomfort to passengers on Summit curves. The only problem is designing summit curves is to provide adequate sight distances.
Circular summit curve is ideal curve as the sight distance available throughout the length of circular > curve is constant. The deviation angles in vertical curves of highways are very small and so between the same tangent points, a simple parabola is nearly congruent with a circular arc; also a parabola is very easy for arithmetical manipulation for computing ordinates. Thus, in actual practice a simple parabolic curve is used as a summit curve instead of the circular arc.

explanationHtml:
Tentative capacity values of urban roads suggested by IRC are:
(i) One way two lane road with no frontage access, no standing vehicles and very little cross traffic - 2400 PCU per hour.
(ii) One way two lane road with frontage access, but no standing vehicle and high capacity intersections - 1500 PCU per hour.
(iii) One way two lane road with free frontage access, parked vehicles and heavy cross traffic - 1200 PCU per hour.
explanationText: Tentative capacity values of urban roads suggested by IRC are: (i) One way two lane road with no frontage access, no standing vehicles and very little cross traffic - 2400 PCU per hour. (iii) One way two lane road with free frontage access, parked vehicles and heavy cross traffic - 1200 PCU per hour.

questionText: A vehicle moving at 60 kmph on an ascending gradient of a highway has to come to stop position to avoid collision with a stationary object. The ratio of lag to brake distance is 6:5. Considering total reaction time of the driver as 2.5 seconds and the coefficient of longitudinal friction as 0.36, the value of ascending gradient(%) is

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \text { Lag distance } &=0.278 \mathrm{Vt} \\ &=0.278 \times 60 \times 2.5 \\ &=41.7 \mathrm{m} \\ \text { Brake distance }&=\frac{5}{6} \times 41.7=34.75 \mathrm{m} \\ &\left[\because \frac{\text { Lag distance }}{\text { Braking distance }}=\frac{6}{5}\right] \\ \text { Braking distance } &=\frac{V^{2}}{254(f+0.01 n)}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 34.75&=\frac{(60)^{2}}{254(0.36+0.01 n)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.01 n&=\frac{(60)^{2}}{254 \times 34.75}-0.36 \\ \Rightarrow \quad n&=4.8 \% \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned} \text { Lag distance } &=0.278 \mathrm{Vt} \\ &=0.278 \times 60 \times 2.5 \\ &=41.7 \mathrm{m} \\ \text { Brake distance }&=\frac{5}{6} \times 41.7=34.75 \mathrm{m} \\ &\left[\because \frac{\text { Lag distance }}{\text { Braking distance }}=\frac{6}{5}\right] \\ \text { Braking distance } &=\frac{V^{2}}{254(f+0.01 n)}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 34.75&=\frac{(60)^{2}}{254(0.36+0.01 n)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.01 n&=\frac{(60)^{2}}{254 \times 34.75}-0.36 \\ \Rightarrow \quad n&=4.8 \% \end{aligned}

The most critical stress value for this pavement is
questionText: For a 25 cm thick cement concrete pavement, analysis of stresses gives the following values : Wheel load stress due to corner loading : 30 kg/c $m^{2}$ Wheel load stress due to edge loading : 32 kg/c $m^{2}$ Warping stress at corner region during summer : 9 kg/c $m^{2}$ Warping stress at corner region during winter : 7 kg/c $m^{2}$ Warping stress at edge region during summer : 8 kg/c $m^{2}$ Warping stress at edge region during summer : 6 kg/c $m^{2}$ Frictional stress during summer : 5 kg/c $m^{2}$ Frictional stress during winter : 4 kg/c $m^{2}$ The most critical stress value for this pavement is

options.html: 40kg/cm2kg/cm^{2}kg/cm2
42kg/cm2kg/cm^{2}kg/cm2
44kg/cm2kg/cm^{2}kg/cm2
45kg/cm2kg/cm^{2}kg/cm2

explanationHtml:
There are four cases which should be considered:
(i) - During summer, critical combination of stresses at edges
=wheel load stress due to edge loading
+warping stress at edge region during summer
- frictional stress during summer
=32+8−5=35 kg/cm2 = 32 + 8 - 5 = 35\text{ kg/cm}^{2}=32+8−5=35 kg/cm2
(ii) During winter, critical combination of stresses at edges.
=wheel load stress due to edge loading
+warping stress at edge region during winter
+ frictional stress during winter
=32+6+4=42kg/cm2 =32 + 6 + 4 = 42 \text{kg/cm}^{2}=32+6+4=42kg/cm2
(iii) During summer, critical combination of stresses at corner regions
=wheel load stress at cor,ner loading
+ warping stress at corner region during
summer
=30+9=39kg/cm2 =30 +9=39 \text{kg/cm}^{2}=30+9=39kg/cm2
(iv) During winter, critical combination of stresses at corner region
=wheel load stress at corner loading
+ Warping stress at corner region during winter
=30+7=37kg/cm2 =30+7=37 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} =30+7=37kg/cm2
Hence, the critical combination is
42kg/cm2 42 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} 42kg/cm2
explanationText: There are four cases which should be considered: (i) - During summer, critical combination of stresses at edges =wheel load stress due to edge loading +warping stress at edge region during summer - frictional stress during summer $= 32 + 8 - 5 = 35\text{ kg/cm}^{2}$ (ii) During winter, critical combination of stresses at edges. =wheel load stress due to edge loading +warping stress at edge region during winter + frictional stress during winter $=32 + 6 + 4 = 42 \text{kg/cm}^{2}$ (iii) During summer, critical combination of stresses at corner regions =wheel load stress at cor,ner loading + warping stress at corner region during summer $=30 +9=39 \text{kg/cm}^{2}$ (iv) During winter, critical combination of stresses at corner region =wheel load stress at corner loading + Warping stress at corner region during winter $=30+7=37 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ Hence, the critical combination is $42 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$

questionText: The design speed for a National Highway is 100 kmph. If the maximum permissible superelevation is 0.10 and the coefficient of lateral friction is 0.15, the ruling minimum radius of horizontal curve on the highway should be
explanationHtml:

Rmin⁡=V2127(θ+f)=(100)2127(0.10+0.15)=314.96m≃315m \begin{aligned} R_{\min } &=\frac{V^{2}}{127(\theta+f)} \\ &=\frac{(100)^{2}}{127(0.10+0.15)} \\ &=314.96 \mathrm{m} \simeq 315 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}Rmin​​=127(θ+f)V2​=127(0.10+0.15)(100)2​=314.96m≃315m​
explanationText: The ruling minimum radius of horizontal curve is given by, $\begin{aligned} R_{\min } &=\frac{V^{2}}{127(\theta+f)} \\ &=\frac{(100)^{2}}{127(0.10+0.15)} \\ &=314.96 \mathrm{m} \simeq 315 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$

questionText: Temperature stresses in concrete pavements may cause the slab to crack. If a slab cools uniformly then the crack will develop at the which of the following locations of the slab ?
explanationHtml:
The corners and edges are free to contract while
cooling. Hence, the cracks due to stresses will
develop at the centre of the slab.
explanationText: The corners and edges are free to contract while cooling. Hence, the cracks due to stresses will develop at the centre of the slab.

questionText: The radius of relatives stiffness for a 20 cm thick slab with $E = 3 \times 10^{5} kg/cm^{2}$ and poisson's ratio = 0.15, resting on a subgrade having modulus of 5 kg/ $cm^{3}$ is
explanationHtml: Given, h=20cm,E=3×105kg/cm2μ=0.15,k=5kg/cm3L=[Eh312k(1−μ2)]1/4=[3×105×20312×5[1−(0.15)2]]1/479.98cm≈80cm\begin{array}{l} \text { Given, } h=20 \mathrm{cm}, E=3 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \\ \mu=0.15, k=5 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} \\ \qquad \begin{aligned} L &=\left[\frac{E h^{3}}{12 k\left(1-\mu^{2}\right)}\right]^{1 / 4} \\ &=\left[\frac{3 \times 10^{5} \times 20^{3}}{12 \times 5\left[1-(0.15)^{2}\right]}\right]^{1 / 4}\\ &79.98cm\approx80cm \end{aligned} \end{array} Given, h=20cm,E=3×105kg/cm2μ=0.15,k=5kg/cm3L​=[12k(1−μ2)Eh3​]1/4=[12×5[1−(0.15)2]3×105×203​]1/479.98cm≈80cm​​
explanationText: $\begin{array}{l} \text { Given, } h=20 \mathrm{cm}, E=3 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \\ \mu=0.15, k=5 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} \\ \qquad \begin{aligned} L &=\left[\frac{E h^{3}}{12 k\left(1-\mu^{2}\right)}\right]^{1 / 4} \\ &=\left[\frac{3 \times 10^{5} \times 20^{3}}{12 \times 5\left[1-(0.15)^{2}\right]}\right]^{1 / 4}\\ &79.98cm\approx80cm \end{aligned} \end{array}$
explanationTex: \begin{array}{l} \text { Given, } h=20 \mathrm{cm}, E=3 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \\ \mu=0.15, k=5 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} \\ \qquad \begin{aligned} L &=\left[\frac{E h^{3}}{12 k\left(1-\mu^{2}\right)}\right]^{1 / 4} \\ &=\left[\frac{3 \times 10^{5} \times 20^{3}}{12 \times 5\left[1-(0.15)^{2}\right]}\right]^{1 / 4}\\ &79.98cm\approx80cm \end{aligned} \end{array}
